lessons.title: From site analysis to design plan
lessons.html:
The design process

Implementing a permaculture design starts with a good plan. A common framework is: observe, analyse, design, implement, maintain and evaluate. Skipping observation is the most common reason designs fail.

Site survey and base map

Draw a base map to scale showing boundaries, buildings, roads, fences, existing trees, water sources, pipes and power lines. Add:

  • Contours and slope direction
  • Soil types and depths from test holes
  • Water flows, ponding areas and erosion
  • Sun path in summer and winter, shade from buildings and trees
  • Prevailing winds, including hot berg winds where relevant
  • Frost pockets (cold air drains to low points)
  • Fire risk direction
  • Access paths and how people move around

Client or community needs

List what the site must provide: vegetables, fruit, eggs, fodder, firewood, income, a training space, shade. Record available labour, budget, skills and water.

Design elements and placement

Use zones (by frequency of use) and sectors (external energies) to place elements:

  • Zone 1: kitchen garden, herbs, nursery, compost and worm farm near the house or work centre.
  • Zone 2: food forest or orchard, poultry house, water tanks.
  • Zone 3: field crops, fodder, larger livestock.
  • Zones 4 and 5: woodlot, natural veld, wildlife corridors.

Place water harvesting (swales, ponds, tanks) high on the site where possible so water can be distributed by gravity. Place windbreaks across the prevailing wind. Check every element for several functions and links: for example, a poultry run below the orchard uses fallen fruit, controls pests and supplies manure.

Implementation plan

Phase the work: water and earthworks first, then access and structures, then soil building, then perennial planting, then annual beds and animals. Prepare a schedule, budget, materials list and labour plan for each phase.

lessons.title: Installing, maintaining and evaluating the design
lessons.html:
Phase 1: Water and earthworks

  • Mark contours with an A-frame or level, then dig swales and berms on contour with spillways to handle overflow safely.
  • Install roof gutters, tanks and first-flush diverters.
  • Construct ponds where suitable, and check whether authorisation is needed for dams on watercourses under the National Water Act 36 of 1998.
  • Plant berms immediately with groundcover to stabilise them.

Phase 2: Access and structures

Lay out paths, gates, fences, poultry houses, compost bays and tool storage according to the plan.

Phase 3: Soil building

  • Sheet mulching: cardboard or newspaper over weeds, then layers of manure, compost and straw.
  • Compost heaps and worm farms.
  • Green manure crops such as legumes to add nitrogen and biomass.

Phase 4: Planting

  • Plant support species first: windbreaks, nitrogen-fixing trees and pioneer plants.
  • Plant fruit trees as guilds, with companions such as comfrey, herbs that attract beneficial insects, and groundcovers.
  • Establish annual beds in Zone 1 with crop rotation and companion planting.
  • Use indigenous and locally adapted species wherever possible; never plant listed invasive species.

Phase 5: Animals

Introduce poultry, ducks or small livestock once fencing, shelter, water and feed are ready, with a welfare and rotation plan.

Maintenance

  • Keep mulch topped up and soil covered.
  • Check swales and spillways after rain.
  • Prune, harvest, save seed and propagate.
  • Monitor pests and use biological controls first.

Evaluation

Record yields, water use, inputs bought, labour hours and observations. Take fixed-point photographs. Compare results with the original goals and adjust the design: permaculture treats feedback as a design principle.

Safety

Earthworks: watch for buried services, avoid undercutting banks and keep children away from ponds or fence them. Use tools and machinery safely and wear PPE.

Key points

  • Observe and map the site before designing.
  • Place elements using zones, sectors and multiple functions.
  • Implement in phases: water first, then structures, soil, plants and animals.
  • Use indigenous or adapted species; avoid invasive plants.
  • Monitor, record and adjust the design over time.
